title: Bid, Ask, Spread and Liquidity
objectives: Read a two-sided quote and compute mid, quoted spread and spread in basis points
Compute the cost of immediate execution against a limit order book, including walking through depth
Distinguish quoted, effective and realised spreads
Explain the economic forces that widen or tighten spreads and list the dimensions of liquidity
motivation: You can have any price you want in a market, if you are willing to wait, or any immediacy you want, if you are willing to pay. That payment is the bid-ask spread, and it is often the largest single cost a trading strategy bears. A backtest that ignores it turns hypothetical profits into real losses; this lesson makes the cost explicit and computable.

blocks.md: The **bid** is the highest price someone will pay to buy from you right now; the **ask** (or offer) is the lowest price someone will accept to sell to you right now. If you want to buy *immediately*, you sell yourself nothing, you **lift the ask**. If you want to sell immediately, you **hit the bid**. The dealer or limit-order trader standing on the other side buys low (bid) and sells high (ask); the gap is their compensation for inventory risk and adverse selection, and your cost for demanding immediacy.

The best bid 100.02 and best ask 100.05 are **the touch**. The **mid** is $(100.02 + 100.05)/2 = 100.035$. The **quoted spread** is $100.05 - 100.02 = 0.03$ - three cents, or $0.03 / 100.035 = 0.0002999 \approx 3.0$ basis points of mid. Note the asymmetric gap: the quote is not centred on any 'true price'; the mid is just a convention, and it moves as either side improves.

blocks.caption: Liquidity is a book you can see: depth stacked at prices away from the touch. The spread is the toll for immediacy; the depth behind it is the road.

blocks.text: Paying the spread: an immediate round trip

blocks.title: Buy 1,000 shares and instantly sell them
items: Buy 1,000 at the ask: $1{,}000 \times 100.05 = \$100{,}050$ (the 1,500-share queue at 100.05 absorbs it).
Annualise the idea: trade in and out weekly and the spread alone eats roughly $52 \times 30 = \$1{,}560$ per year on a \$100k position, before any price movement.

blocks.title: Three spreads you should know
blocks.md: **Quoted spread**: ask minus bid at the touch, a book property. **Effective spread**: $2 \times |\text{trade price} - \text{mid at trade time}|$ - what you *actually* paid on a fill. **Realised spread**: effective spread minus subsequent price drift - what the liquidity provider kept after the market moved. They differ whenever your order walks through depth or the mid moves between quote and fill.

blocks.text: Depth: when your order does not fit at the touch

blocks.md: Liquidity is not just the top of book, it is the **depth** behind it. A market buy of 2,000 shares here cannot fill at 100.05 (only 1,500 available): it takes 1,500 at 100.05 plus 500 at 100.06. Cost $= 1{,}500 \times 100.05 + 500 \times 100.06 = 150{,}075 + 50{,}030 = 200{,}105$, so the **VWAP** (volume-weighted average price) is $200{,}105 / 2{,}000 = 100.0525$ - a quarter of a cent above the touch, on average. That extra cost is **market impact**, and it grows disproportionately with order size: doubling your size can more than double your impact when the book is thin.

The symmetrical experiment on the sell side: dumping 2,300 shares walks the bids ($1{,}200 \times 100.02 + 800 \times 100.01 + 300 \times 100.00$), recovering only \$230,032 for shares bought at \$230,123, a 91-dollar immediate loss before the market even moves. Illiquidity is a tax charged in both directions.

items: **Volatility**: an unfilled inventory can move against the provider; wilder stocks need wider protection.
**Adverse selection**: counterparties who know more than the quoter hit the stale side; the wider the information gap (news pending, earnings), the wider the spread.
**Competition and tick size**: more competing quoters compress spreads; the minimum increment (typically \$0.01 for US listed equities above \$1) sets a floor.
**Inventory and capital costs**: funding positions and balance-sheet usage are real costs priced into the quote.

blocks.md: Liquidity itself has four dimensions worth naming, because different trading styles stress different ones: **tightness** (narrow spread), **depth** (size at the touch and beyond), **resilience** (how fast the book refills after a large trade) and **immediacy** (how fast you can trade at all). A stock can be tight and shallow, or deep and wide; strategy sizing must respect all four, not just the top-of-book spread.

guidedExercise.prompt: Using the order book in the lesson (bids: 1,200 at 100.02, 800 at 100.01, 500 at 100.00; asks: 1,500 at 100.05, 900 at 100.06), a trader buys 1,200 shares at the market and immediately sells all 1,200 at the market. Compute both legs and the round-trip loss.
hints: 1,200 fits entirely within the 1,500 shares at the ask, so the buy fills at one price.
On the sell side, 1,200 fits within the 1,200 shares at the bid.
guidedExercise.solution: Buy: $1{,}200 \times 100.05 = \$120{,}060$. Sell: $1{,}200 \times 100.02 = \$120{,}024$. Loss $= 36$, which is again spread $\times$ size: $0.03 \times 1{,}200$. Because both sides fit at the touch, the cost is exactly the quoted spread, walking through depth only begins beyond 1,500 shares.

independentExercise.prompt: A trader market-buys 2,300 shares from the lesson's book, then market-sells all 2,300 a moment later with no price change. (a) Compute the buy VWAP and total cost. (b) Compute the sell proceeds by walking down the bids. (c) What is the total round-trip loss, and what was the average cost per share of demanding immediacy?
hints: Sell: 1,200 at 100.02, then 800 at 100.01, then the remaining 300 at 100.00.
Loss divided by shares bought is the average immediacy cost.
independentExercise.solution: (a) Buy cost $= 1{,}500 \times 100.05 + 800 \times 100.06 = 150{,}075 + 80{,}048 = \$230{,}123$; VWAP $= 230{,}123/2{,}300 = 100.053478$. (b) Sell proceeds $= 1{,}200 \times 100.02 + 800 \times 100.01 + 300 \times 100.00 = 120{,}024 + 80{,}008 + 30{,}000 = \$230{,}032$. (c) Loss $= 230{,}123 - 230{,}032 = \textbf{\$91.00}$, i.e. $91/2{,}300 \approx 3.96$ cents per share, nearly the full four-cent effective spread on both sides, larger than the 3-cent quoted spread because depth was consumed.

commonMistakes: Assuming the full order fills at the touch: sizes beyond displayed depth fill at worse prices.
Reading the bid as the price you buy at, you buy at the ask and sell at the bid.
Quoting the spread in cents across stocks at very different price levels without converting to basis points.
Treating the mid as a tradable price: no one trades at the mid; it is a reference point, not a fill.
realWorldApplication: Execution desks monitor quoted and effective spreads in real time; retail platforms disclose effective spread costs; venue selection (lit exchange vs dark pool vs wholesaler) is largely a spread-and-impact decision.
quantFinanceApplication: Backtests must charge realistic spread and impact costs: a strategy whose simulated gross edge is smaller than twice the spread it pays per round trip is guaranteed to lose money after costs, regardless of its statistical beauty.
summary: You buy at the ask and sell at the bid; the quoted spread (here \$0.03, about 3 bps) is the price of immediacy.
An immediate round trip costs spread × size exactly when both sides fill at the touch (\$30 on 1,000 shares at 100.02/100.05).
Orders larger than displayed depth walk the book: 2,000 shares bought here average 100.0525 (VWAP), paying market impact beyond the spread.
Spreads widen with volatility, adverse selection and inventory costs; liquidity has four dimensions, tightness, depth, resilience and immediacy.

quiz.prompt: A stock is quoted 50.10 bid / 50.14 ask. What is the quoted spread in basis points of the mid (to two decimals)?
You want to buy 500 shares immediately. At which price do you trade?
quiz.explanation: Immediate buys lift the ask. The bid is where immediate *sellers* trade; the mid is a reference nobody trades at.

quiz.prompt: A spread of \$0.02 applies to both sides of a trade of 500 shares. What is the total round-trip cost of buying and immediately selling (in dollars)?
quiz.explanation: Round-trip cost $= \text{spread} \times \text{size} = 0.02 \times 500 = 10$, assuming both sides fill at the touch.

quiz.prompt: Which situations tend to *widen* the bid-ask spread?
options: Earnings news about to be released
A deep, heavily traded large-cap with many competing market makers
A market maker with a large, hard-to-hedge inventory position
quiz.explanation: Information asymmetry, volatility and inventory risk all raise the provider's cost of quoting tight. Competition among many quoters is the main force that *narrows* spreads.

quiz.prompt: Define depth and explain in one sentence why two stocks with identical spreads can still differ dramatically in liquidity.
quiz.modelAnswer: Depth is the size available at and near the best bid and ask; two stocks can share a tight top-of-book spread while one supports large orders without moving (deep) and the other moves violently on modest size (shallow).
quiz.explanation: Spread measures the price of immediacy at small size; depth and impact determine what happens to larger trades, and resilience determines how fast the book recovers.

quiz.prompt: What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
book = [(1500, 100.05), (900, 100.06)]
qty, cost = 0, 0.0
for size, price in book:
    take = min(size, 2000 - qty)
    cost += take * price
    qty += take
    if qty >= 2000:
        break
print(round(cost / qty, 4))
quiz.explanation: The loop walks the asks: 1,500 at 100.05 then 500 at 100.06, total 200,105 for 2,000 shares. VWAP $= 100.0525$, exactly the lesson's worked example.

flashcards.back: Bid: best price you can sell to now. Ask: best price you can buy from now. Mid = (bid+ask)/2. Quoted spread = ask, bid (here \$0.03 ≈ 3 bps on 100.035).
Cost = spread × size when both sides fill at the touch: 0.03 × 1,000 shares = \$30.

flashcards.front: Quoted vs effective vs realised spread
flashcards.back: Quoted: book property at the touch. Effective: 2 × |fill − mid at trade time| (what you paid). Realised: effective minus subsequent drift (what the provider kept).
Tightness (narrow spread), depth (size behind the touch), resilience (book refills after trades), immediacy (speed of execution).
